alt: Field Lines from a Positive Charge. E points away from a positive source charge.
Field Lines from a Negative Charge. E points toward a negative source charge.
Field Lines Never Cross. Field lines do not cross: the net electric field is a single vector at each point.
Single Point Charge. A single charge creates a radial electric field.
Two Like Charges. For equal positive charges, the midpoint has zero net electric field.
Two Opposite Charges (Dipole). Dipole field lines run from the positive charge to the negative charge.
Multiple Charges (Complex). The net field combines the vector contributions of all source charges.
Movement of Positive Test Charges. A positive charge released from rest accelerates along E; its electric potential energy falls.
Movement of Negative Test Charges. A negative charge released from rest accelerates opposite E; its electric potential energy also falls.
High vs. Low Electric Potential. Potential decreases along E. Potential energy depends on both potential and charge.
Parallel Plate Capacitor. Between large parallel plates, the field is nearly uniform away from edges.
Varying Plate Separation. Fixed Q and plate area: E stays approximately constant while V = Ed increases with separation.
Electric Potential Maps. An equipotential is perpendicular to E; moving along it changes no electric potential energy.
Energy Stored. A charged capacitor stores electric potential energy in its electric field.
Conductors. At electrostatic equilibrium, excess charge is on the surface; only special shapes are uniform.
Insulators. In an insulator, added charge does not freely spread across the object.
Surface Charge and Charge Concentration. Sharp curvature can concentrate surface charge and strengthen the local field.
Polarization in Conductors. Mobile electrons redistribute within a neutral conductor.
Polarization in Insulators. Bound charges shift within molecules; electrons do not flow freely across the insulator.
Attraction of Neutral Objects. Opposite charge is nearer the rod, so attraction can exceed the more distant repulsion.
No Net Charge Transfer. Polarization redistributes charge inside an object without transferring net charge across the gap.
Charge Concentration on Sharp Points. Sharper conducting surfaces can have stronger local electric fields.
Electrostatic Discharge. A sufficiently strong electric field can ionize air and allow a discharge.
Lightning Rods. A bonded conductor routes lightning current toward ground; it does not stop every strike.
Electron Drift: The Slow Journey. Slow electron drift differs from the much faster propagation of an electric signal.
Conventional vs. Actual Electron Flow. In metal wires, electron drift is opposite conventional current.
What is Charge Flow?. Current is the rate at which net charge crosses a section of the conductor.
Wire Length. Same material and area: doubling wire length doubles resistance.
Wire Thickness. Same material and length: doubling cross-sectional area halves resistance.
Material Type. Compare wires of equal length, area, and temperature to isolate material resistivity.
Temperature. For ordinary metals, resistance usually rises as temperature rises.
Open Circuit. An open path stops steady current in this simple DC circuit.
Closed Circuit. A complete path allows current through the load.
Short Circuit. A low-resistance bypass can draw excessive current. This is a fault diagram, not a build instruction.
Ammeter. The ammeter carries the same branch current as the load.
Voltmeter. The voltmeter connects to the two ends of the load to compare their potentials.
Adding in Series. Series resistances add; at fixed supply voltage the current decreases.
Adding in Parallel. Adding a parallel branch lowers equivalent resistance and increases total current at fixed voltage.
Equivalent Resistance Formulae. Use a direct sum for series and a reciprocal sum for parallel resistors.
Broken Series Path. One break interrupts the only series path.
Broken Parallel Branch. A break in one parallel branch leaves the other complete path available.
Short Circuit. A short bypasses the intended load through a low-resistance path.
Ammeter in Series. Use a low-resistance ammeter in series with the measured branch.
Ammeter in Parallel. Incorrect: a low-resistance ammeter across a load creates an unwanted bypass.
Voltmeter Across Branches. Use a high-resistance voltmeter across the two points being compared.
Voltmeter in Series. Incorrect: a voltmeter in series greatly reduces the current.
Oersted’s Discovery. A compass near a current-carrying wire responds to the wire’s magnetic field.
Magnetic Field Around a Straight Wire. Right-hand rule: thumb follows conventional current; curled fingers show B.
Magnetic Field Patterns. Reversing the current reverses the circular magnetic-field direction.
Current. With the same coil and core, greater current generally strengthens the magnetic field.
Coil Turns. More turns can strengthen the field at fixed current; a fixed battery adds a resistance tradeoff.
Core Material. An iron core can strengthen the field without changing the circuit current.
Distance. Keep pickup distance and method fixed when comparing lifting performance.
What Makes a Good Scientific Question?. Ask how a specified change affects a measurable result.
Choosing Variables. Independent: current. Dependent: clips. Controls: coil, core, wire, and pickup method.
Planning a Fair Test. A fair comparison changes one intended variable while keeping relevant conditions fixed.
Making Predictions. Record a reasoned prediction before examining the result.
Measuring Magnetic Strength. Clips lifted measure lifting performance; they are not a direct measurement of B in tesla.
Repeating Trials. Physical repeats reveal variation. Identical inputs in a deterministic model may repeat exactly.
Controlling Uncertainty. Control physical measurement conditions; evaluate simulation limits without inventing random failures.
Recording Data. Record the settings, displayed outputs, and comparison measure for each design.
Reading Data Tables. Keep all six fictional raw measurements and show means in a separate column.
Constructing and Interpreting Graphs. Plot current on the horizontal axis and clip count on the vertical axis.
Identifying Patterns and Trends. Two tested settings support a comparison, not a universal proportional law.
Comparing Multiple Trials. Compare means and the spread of repeated observations.
Current and lifting performance. The invented mean rises from 10 to 19 clips; this is not an exact doubling law.
Turns, current, and cost. More lifting does not automatically mean better clips per cost.
Core Material Comparisons. Compare core materials while holding the circuit settings fixed.
Limits and improvements. Preserve inconvenient observations and propose a specific way to improve the evidence.
Strength of Magnetic Field. For the same changing-field pattern and geometry, a larger change rate produces a larger emf.
Area of the Coil. For the same uniform dB/dt and orientation, a larger loop area gives a larger induced emf.
Number of Turns in Coil. Same flux change per turn: doubling the turns doubles the induced emf.
Speed of Motion. Faster change of flux produces a larger induced emf; current also depends on circuit resistance.
Orientation of Coil. For steady rotation, flux is largest when emf is zero; emf is largest when flux passes through zero.
Magnet Entering a Coil. An approaching north pole induces a near north face, opposing the increasing flux.
Magnet Leaving a Coil. A receding north pole induces a near south face, opposing the decreasing flux.
Reversing Magnet Polarity. An approaching south pole induces a near south face; the induced current reverses.
Conservation of Energy. Mechanical work supplies the electrical energy and losses in a loaded generator.
Number of Coil Turns. At fixed current, field, area, and angle, more turns give greater torque.
Current Strength. At fixed field, geometry, and angle, greater current gives greater torque.
Magnetic Field Strength. A stronger field increases torque with other factors held fixed; efficiency does not follow automatically.
Coil Orientation. Motor torque depends on the angle between the coil normal and magnetic field.
Commutator Function. A split-ring commutator reverses the coil connection every half-turn in a simple DC motor.
Rotation Speed. For a uniform field and fixed coil, doubling rotation speed doubles peak emf.
Magnetic Field Strength. At fixed rotation speed and geometry, doubling B doubles peak emf.
Number of Coil Turns. More turns increase emf; the resulting current also depends on total resistance and load.
Coil Area. At fixed rotation rate, turns, and field, a larger coil area increases peak emf.
Type of Current Produced (AC/DC). Slip rings give alternating output; a split-ring commutator can give pulsating DC.
Motor. A motor transfers electrical energy into useful mechanical energy and other forms.
Generator. A generator transfers mechanical energy into electrical energy and other forms.
Electrical Resistance. Current through resistance transfers electrical energy into thermal energy at a rate I²R.
Friction. Friction in moving contacts transfers mechanical energy into thermal energy.
Heat Production. Heating changes where energy goes; it does not destroy energy.
Sound Energy. Vibrating parts transfer some energy to sound in the surroundings.
Eddy Currents. Insulated laminations interrupt large eddy-current loops and can reduce unwanted heating.
Number of Coil Turns. Extra turns add field contribution, wire resistance, and cost; compare actual performance.
Core Material. Core material affects field strength, losses, and cost.
Battery Voltage (Input Energy). Voltage is energy per charge; at fixed resistance, greater voltage gives greater current.
Wire Resistance. At the same current, lower wire resistance reduces I²R heating.
Device Size and Weight. Design size trades off capacity, material use, mass, and available space.
Cost Constraints. Choose a design by comparing performance against a stated budget and constraints.
Electromagnetic Crane. A powered coil magnetizes the core to lift suitable magnetic materials.
Electric Generator. Rotation changes flux linkage and produces electrical output.
Magnetic Braking System. Eddy currents oppose relative motion and transfer kinetic energy into thermal energy.
Dynamic Microphone. Sound moves the diaphragm and coil; changing flux linkage produces a small signal voltage.
